orient: Narrator: Nelly Dean, still telling Lockwood her story. It carries straight on from the end of Chapter VIII, the same day in about 1780, as Hindley comes home drunk. After the asterisks at the very end, Lockwood's own diary takes over briefly.

notes.m: Not 'admiring'. Something 'impressed' on you is pressed in deep, like a stamp.

notes.t: by the skin of my neck
notes.g: By the scruff of my neck.
Mr. Kenneth, the local doctor (Chapter VIII).
A local bog, probably invented by the author.
Herrings salted and smoked until red, strong-smelling and cheap.
notes.n: Nelly coolly jokes that the knife will taste of fish.
'Unnatural' means lacking the natural love of a child for its father.
'Thee', 'thou' and 'thy' were the familiar forms of 'you', used by northern country people to children and family.
People cropped dogs' ears to make them look fiercer. Hindley's drunken talk is about cutting the boy's ears.

notes.t: devilish conceit it is, to cherish our ears—we’re asses enough without them
notes.g: It's vanity to keep our ears: we're fools enough already.
notes.n: A drunken joke: donkeys (asses) have long ears, and 'ass' also means fool.

notes.m: Making a sign with her hand, not writing a signature.

notes.g: The person who caused the accident.
A stingy person who hoards money.

notes.t: a lucky lottery ticket for five shillings
notes.g: A winning lottery ticket, sold off for a quarter of a pound.
notes.n: Britain ran state lotteries in the 1700s. Twenty shillings made a pound.

notes.g: A huge fortune, many lifetimes of a servant's wages.

notes.t: the instrument of thwarting his own revenge
notes.g: The means of spoiling his own revenge.
notes.n: In Chapter VII Heathcliff swore to pay Hindley back. Without thinking, he has saved Hindley's only son.

notes.g: The precious child in my care.

notes.m: 'Idiot' was then a term for a person with a severe mental disability, not just an insult.

notes.g: Someone who is not a Christian; a godless person.

notes.t: a pretty state you’re come to
notes.g: A fine state you've got into (said ironically).
notes.m: 'Pretty' here is sarcastic: a terrible state.

notes.g: The man who had gone so badly astray.
As I happen to feel like it.
A bottle holding a pint (a little over half a litre) of brandy.
The sideboard with shelves for dishes.
To punish God, who made his soul.
notes.n: Hindley's blasphemy: he would damn himself just to spite God.

notes.g: A drinking toast to his own soul going to hell.
His strong body won't give in.
A long wooden bench with a high back.
notes.n: Its tall back hides whoever is on the other side. Keep track of who can see whom.

notes.s: It was far in the night
notes.tr: It was late in the night, and the little children were crying. Their mother, under the earth of her grave, heard them.
notes.n: From 'The Ghaist's Warning', an old Danish ballad translated into Scots in the early 1800s. In it a dead mother rises from her grave to protect her mistreated children. A pointed song for Hareton, whose mother is dead.

notes.g: The scene you made (slapping Nelly and Edgar in Chapter VIII).

notes.t: You have pledged your word, and cannot retract
notes.g: You've given your promise and can't take it back.
notes.n: An engagement was a serious promise. A man could even be sued for breaking one ('breach of promise').
Like the church catechism, a set of questions and fixed answers that children learned by heart.

notes.t: for a girl of twenty-two it was not injudicious
notes.g: For a young woman of twenty-two (Nelly herself), this was quite wise.
notes.n: Nelly is congratulating her younger self. 'Injudicious' means unwise. Catherine is only about fifteen.

notes.g: Getting there; that one is neither good nor bad.

notes.m: Not a circus clown. A 'clown' was an ill-mannered, uneducated rustic.

notes.g: Edgar's parents, Mr. and Mrs. Linton.

notes.t: in whichever place the soul lives
notes.g: Wherever the soul lives, in the head or in the heart.
Calling up, as if by magic.

notes.m: 'Oblige' here means force, not do a favour.

notes.g: Believing that dreams can foretell the future.
notes.n: A common country belief. Nelly is afraid of what this dream might predict.

notes.g: The open moorland of heather and grass.
Pushed Heathcliff so far down in the world.
notes.n: Hindley has made him an uneducated farm labourer.

notes.t: It would degrade me to marry Heathcliff now
notes.g: Marrying Heathcliff would lower my social position.
notes.n: He has no money, no family name and works as a servant.

notes.m: 'Sensible of' means conscious of, not reasonable.
'Remark' here means notice, not comment on.

notes.g: Luckily, at just the right moment.

notes.n: He has been carting lime at Penistone Crags all day (Chapter VIII).

notes.t: As soon as you become Mrs. Linton
notes.g: As soon as you marry Edgar Linton.

notes.t: They’ll meet the fate of Milo!
notes.n: Milo of Croton was a famous ancient Greek wrestler. In old age he tried to tear apart a split tree trunk with his hands; it closed on them, trapping him, and wolves ate him. Catherine means that whoever tries to part them will come to a bad end.
Heathcliff has nothing, and Catherine can expect little from Hindley.

notes.g: Help Heathcliff go up in the world.
Nelly's point: the money would be Edgar's, not hers.
notes.n: Under English law then, a wife's property passed to her husband, so she would have little money of her own.

notes.g: The walled farmyard or animal pen.

notes.s: And how isn’t that nowt comed in
notes.tr: How come that good-for-nothing hasn't come in from the field by now? What is he up to? The great idle lump!

notes.t: ill eneugh for ony fahl manners
notes.g: Wicked enough for any foul behaviour.

notes.m: 'Meat' meant food in general, not only flesh.

notes.g: The prayer of thanks said before or after eating.
The upper floor of a barn or stable, where hay is stored.

notes.n: Ferrets were used to chase rabbits out of their burrows.

notes.s: Yon lad gets war und war!
notes.e: out of his heead for nowt!
notes.tr: That lad gets worse and worse! He's left the gate wide open, and Miss's pony has trampled down two ridges of corn and floundered right through into the meadow! Well, the master will raise the devil tomorrow, and he'll be right to. He's patience itself with such careless, worthless creatures, patience itself he is! But he won't always be like that, you'll see, all of you! You mustn't drive him out of his mind for nothing!

notes.n: 'Rigs' are the raised strips of a ploughed field. 'Corn' in Britain means wheat, oats or barley, not maize.
'Offald' is related to 'offal', the waste parts of a slaughtered animal.

notes.s: I sud more likker look for th’ horse
notes.e: less hard o’ hearing wi’ ye!
notes.tr: I'd more likely look for the horse. That would make more sense. But I can't look for either horse or man on a night like this, as black as the chimney! And Heathcliff's not the sort to come when I whistle. Maybe he'll be less hard of hearing with you!

notes.g: Not the fellow; not the sort.

notes.n: Still heard in Yorkshire: 'happen he will'.

notes.g: A large branch of a tree.
The column of brick or stone chimneys rising above the roof.
Two good men in the Bible whom God spared when He destroyed the wicked.
notes.n: Noah survived the Flood in his ark (Genesis 6–9). Lot escaped when God rained fire on the city of Sodom (Genesis 19).

notes.g: The sinner bringing bad luck on everyone.
notes.n: In the Bible, God sends a storm against Jonah's ship because Jonah is running away from Him. The sailors throw Jonah overboard, and the sea grows calm.

notes.g: His room (like a wild animal's lair).

notes.t: a wide distinction might be drawn between saints like himself and sinners like his master
notes.g: Joseph is sure God would spare him and punish Hindley.
notes.n: As a Calvinist, Joseph counts himself among the saved. Hindley's curses only confirm to him that the master is damned.

notes.s: Nay, nay, he’s noan at Gimmerton
notes.tr: No, no, he's not at Gimmerton. I wouldn't be surprised if he's at the bottom of a bog-hole. This visitation wasn't for nothing, and I'd have you watch out, Miss: you may be next. Thank Heaven for everything! All things work together for good to those who are chosen and picked out from the rubbish! You know what the Scripture says.

notes.g: Bog-hole: a deep pool of mud on the moor.
All things work together for good.
notes.n: From Romans 8:28: 'all things work together for good to them that love God'. Joseph twists it to mean good only for the chosen few.
Joseph's Calvinist belief: God has chosen in advance the few who will be saved (the 'elect'). Everyone else is 'rubbish'.

notes.g: Stubborn; set on having her own way.

notes.t: his slow step on the ladder
notes.g: Joseph climbing up to his room under the roof.
notes.n: Attic rooms in old farmhouses were often reached by a ladder.

notes.g: Cracks in the wooden window shutters.
She is very bad; she has behaved wickedly.
notes.m: Stronger then than today's mild word for a child misbehaving.

notes.g: The window, with its small panes set in a crisscross frame.

notes.m: In northern speech 'starving' meant perishing with cold, not hungry.

notes.g: The glowing remains of a fire.

notes.s: Running after t’ lads, as usuald!
notes.tr: Running after the lads, as usual! If I were you, master, I'd just slam the doors in all their faces, gentry and common folk alike! There's never a day you're away but that cat of a Linton comes sneaking over here. And Miss Nelly, she's a fine girl! She sits watching for you in the kitchen, and as you come in at one door, he goes out at the other. And then our grand lady goes courting on her side! Fine behaviour, lurking about the fields after midnight with that foul, frightful devil of a gipsy, Heathcliff! They think I'm blind, but I'm not, nothing of the sort! I saw young Linton both coming and going, and I saw you (to Nelly), you good-for-nothing, slovenly witch, jump up and dash into the house the minute you heard the master's horse's hooves clatter up the road.

notes.n: An old phrase: 'gentle' meant well-born, 'simple' meant humble.
From 'slattern', an untidy woman.

notes.t: he did me a good turn a short time since
notes.g: He did me a favour not long ago.
notes.n: Hindley means Heathcliff catching Hareton when he fell, earlier in this chapter.

notes.t: make my conscience tender of breaking his neck
notes.g: Make me feel guilty about killing him.

notes.t: I shall only have the more humour for you
notes.g: I'll just have more bad temper left over for you.
notes.m: 'Humour' here means mood or temper, not comedy.

notes.g: A raving, confused state, caused here by high fever.
He drew blood from her as a treatment.
notes.n: Bleeding, by cutting a vein or applying leeches, was standard medicine then. Doctors thought it cooled a fever. It actually weakened patients.

notes.g: A sickroom diet of thin liquids.
notes.n: Whey is the watery liquid left over when milk is made into cheese. Water-gruel is thin porridge made with water instead of milk.

notes.g: The district served by the local church, and by the doctor.

notes.t: ceased to hold any communication with me
save in the relation of a mere servant
notes.g: Except as a mistress gives orders to a servant.
Was shut out of her favour too.

notes.m: The older meaning is 'make more serious', not just 'annoying'.

notes.g: A marriage linking the family to the Lintons.
notes.n: The Lintons are richer and grander. Such a match would raise the Earnshaws' standing.

notes.g: Married her at the church in Gimmerton.
notes.n: A 'chapel' could mean a small local church that served part of a large parish.

notes.t: three years subsequent to his father’s death
notes.g: Three years after his father died.
Go with her here to Thrushcross Grange.
notes.n: So this is how Nelly came to live at the Grange, where she is telling the story.

notes.g: Teach him the alphabet; teach him to read.
The first one mentioned: her husband, Edgar.
The second one mentioned: her brother, Hindley.

notes.t: now that there was no mistress
notes.g: Now that Catherine had left, there was no lady of the house at the Heights.

notes.t: the curate should take him in hand
notes.g: The curate would see to his education.
We have been strangers; I've hardly seen him.
notes.n: Lockwood met Hareton at the Heights in Chapter II, a rough, uneducated young man.

notes.g: Very strange to think of it.

notes.n: 'Chimney' here means the fireplace.

notes.g: Put off the next part of the story.

notes.t: aching laziness of head and limbs
notes.n: He predicted 'an obstinate cold' in Chapter VII.
